entry.title: South Africa in Erasmus+: 2,746 outbound and 1,879 inbound mobilities in the last programme, and 600 more student places to Europe from the 2022 selections
entry.summary:
The DHET's international scholarships portal records South Africa's participation in Erasmus+ since 2014 across all the components open to partner countries. Under the 2014 to 2020 programme, International Credit Mobility took 2,746 students and staff from South Africa to Europe and brought 1,879 from Europe to South Africa; 78 South African students won full Erasmus Mundus Joint Master scholarships, 29 capacity-building projects ran with four coordinated by South African institutions, and six Jean Monnet projects and one network were implemented. From the 2022 selections of the 2021 to 2027 programme, the page lists 461 staff mobilities to Europe and 416 from Europe to South Africa, 600 student mobilities to Europe and 128 into South Africa, three new capacity-building projects, ten instances of TVET capacity-building participation and five instances in two virtual exchange projects.

Why it matters here: The national picture into which the Aix-Marseille partnership fits: these figures show that the Wits mobilities are part of an established South African flow with a home department that tracks it, which matters for reporting, for Wits International's dealings with DHET, and for arguing that teacher education deserves a larger share.

Department of Higher Education and Training, International Scholarships portal, Erasmus+ Programme page (consulted 18 September 2026) · Official page of a national government department

entry.title: What the partner already runs: INSPE Aix-Marseille's student mobility page, from Erasmus+ semesters to CIVIS schools and teaching placements abroad
entry.summary:
The Institute of Teaching and Education (INSPE) at Aix-Marseille Université sets out the mobility routes open to its trainee teachers. Erasmus+ study periods last from three to twelve months per study cycle at eleven partner universities in Germany, Belgium, Denmark, Spain, Greece, the Netherlands and Switzerland, with credits validated on return; CIVIS supports study visits to alliance partners, and CIVIS schools offer one- to three-week intensive courses with practical work. Short formats include the International Education Week summer school at Tübingen, taught in English, and a Franco-German musical education exchange with Universität Hamburg. Placement mobility covers Erasmus+ teaching internships of two to twelve months and France Éducation International language-assistant posts of four to twelve months, with grants arranged through the international mobility manager.

Why it matters here: This is the machinery the Wits School of Education will plug into: INSPE already sends and receives trainee teachers on semester exchanges and short CIVIS formats, so the KA171 mobilities can copy its credit validation, its short-course model and its mobility-manager role rather than inventing them.

INSPE Aix-Marseille, International, Student mobility page (consulted 18 September 2026) · Official page of the partner institution

entry.title: Fifty-five educators on what Erasmus staff exchange did for them: leadership, intercultural competence and the barriers that keep others at home
entry.summary:
A qualitative study at Transylvania University of Brașov drew on in-depth interviews with 55 educators from European and non-European countries who had taken part in Erasmus staff exchange, tracing how short-term mobility reshaped their professional practice, career paths and engagement with their institutions. Participants reported gains in intercultural competence, global awareness and pedagogical innovation, and described a renewed sense of purpose and an expanded leadership identity on return. The authors also record persistent barriers, including financial constraints, gaps in language proficiency and uneven institutional support, and argue that unless these are addressed Erasmus will serve the already advantaged rather than transform education systems.

Why it matters here: Evidence for the staff strand of the Wits and Aix-Marseille project: it suggests what to ask returning academics and administrators in the project's own evaluation, and its warning about language and institutional support speaks directly to a partnership working across English and French.

Ivasciuc, Marinescu and Ispas, Education Sciences, volume 15, issue 6, article 712, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY)

entry.title: How Erasmus+ KA171 mobility works: the rules this project runs under
entry.summary:
The Erasmus+ Programme Guide sets the rules for mobility projects for higher education students and staff. Projects supported by external policy funds, the strand this partnership falls under, run for 24 or 36 months, cover every study cycle from short cycle to doctoral, and allow blended mobility that combines a physical stay with a virtual component. Regional rules apply: for Sub-Saharan Africa at least 35% of the budget must go to mobility with the region's least developed countries and no more than 8% to any single country. Partner institutions outside the Programme countries cannot sign the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education but must respect its principles, so fair and transparent selection, recognition of learning outcomes and support for participants have to be made explicit in the inter-institutional agreement.

Why it matters here: The rulebook for this project: the 36-month duration, the doctoral and blended mobility options, and the requirement that selection and recognition be spelt out in the inter-institutional agreement all come from here, which is why the Wits side's first task is that agreement.

European Commission, Erasmus+ Programme Guide, Part B, Key Action 1, mobility projects for higher education students and staff (version consulted 16 September 2026) · Official programme guide of the European Commission

entry.title: CIVIS asks Europe to treat academic mobility from Africa as a visa priority
entry.summary:
CIVIS, the European University Alliance to which Aix-Marseille University belongs and which has African member institutions, has published a position paper on visas for Africa-Europe academic mobility. Drawing on its own surveys, it reports that African applicants face long waiting times, difficulty getting appointments, high costs, long journeys to consulates and heavy documentation, which lead to delayed or cancelled exchanges. It welcomes the European Commission's moves to modernise visa policy and asks for three additions: academic mobility as a priority category with longer-validity, multiple-entry visas; simplified procedures extended to short academic stays such as conferences and research visits; and strategic priority for Africa, with more consular capacity and faster processing.

Why it matters here: The practical risk this project must plan for: a Wits student or colleague holding an Erasmus+ grant still needs a French visa in time, so nomination windows and consulate lead times belong in the mobility calendar from the start, and the CIVIS position gives the partnership a policy argument to cite.

CIVIS position paper and newsroom, 9 September 2026 · Position paper of a European University Alliance, drawing on its own member surveys
